narration.text: One date explains this whole street, and it is eighteen eighty. Before that, the ground under your feet was part of eighty-seven acres owned by Doctor William Aspinwall — and his family had been on this side of Brookline since sixteen fifty, when Peter Aspinwall bought land near what is now Saint Paul and Aspinwall Avenue. Five generations, one hill. In eighteen eighty Dr. Aspinwall sold it, the Aspinwall Hill Land Company formed, and it laid out the roads, the house lots, and the footpaths as one plan. Building started that same year. Every lot line on this street, including the one you're standing on, comes out of that single subdivision.

deep_narration.text: Worth noting what I have not told you: When this particular house was built. I don't know. That is not modesty — the assessor record and the deed chain would settle it in an afternoon, and nobody has looked. I could guess from the houses either side of you and I would probably be close, and 'probably close' is how a wrong date enters the record and stays there. So the honest version is: The land is eighteen eighty or later, and the building is unresearched. There is a hunt item for exactly this.

narration.text: This is Lotta Bradburn Shick Park, and the record here has three dates, not one. The town bought this land in nineteen forty-five. It opened for recreation in nineteen fifty, as Addington Park. It was renamed for her in nineteen fifty-five. An earlier account of this stop compressed all three into "dedicated in nineteen forty-five" — a simplification, not a fabrication, but worth correcting. Shick herself is far better documented than a plaque suggests: A Wellsley College graduate, fifteen years on the School Committee starting in nineteen twenty-nine, a Town Meeting member from nineteen twenty-five, an advocate for school lunch standards and school nursing. She founded the Aspinwall Hill Associates — the neighborhood association for the ground we're standing on — and pushed for Brookline's first municipal golf course. She ran for the state legislature twice and for Selectman once; no source says whether she won any of the three.

conversation_starters.text: Earbuds out for this one. Ask whoever's with you what they'd want on their plaque if it were the only thing left.

narration.text: The town accepted this path in eighteen ninety-four — fourteen years after development began, which tells you the paths were not an afterthought but did take some arguing. It is one of seven on Aspinwall Hill. It runs from Winthrop Road, near the intersection with Colbourne Crescent and Addington Road, up to the Shick Park entrance, climbing the hill in just under two hundred ninety-five feet. Thomas Aspinwall, Doctor Aspinwall's eldest son, was a partner in the engineering firm that drew the plan for the hill, and he pushed to have the paths included. Whether he deserves the credit for them is his biographer's inference, not the record's. What the record says is that he argued for them.

Two hundred and seventy-two words ago I couldn't give you a single hard date for how these hillside paths came to exist. Here is one: October 10, eighteen ninety-three. That's the day Brookline's Selectmen held a special meeting and formally accepted both this path and University Road as public ways, with a ninety-five-dollar — sorry, nine hundred fifty dollar — appropriation for a wooden plank walk. A town meeting minute, not a plaque, not an inference from a map. This path runs from Winthrop Road down to Washington Street, three hundred seventy-nine feet, crossing land Boston University owned before the Aspinwall Hill Land Company bought it in eighteen eighty. Same land deal we've been standing on this whole walk. Different corner of it.
